code.title: Multicast delegate: static, instance and lambda targets

followUps:
Only the value from the last method in the invocation list is returned; the results of earlier methods are thrown away. With Func<int> f = () => 1; f += () => 2;, calling f() runs both but returns 2.

To collect every result, walk the list yourself:

foreach (Func<int> h in f.GetInvocationList())
    Console.WriteLine(h());   // prints 1 then 2

If one method throws, the remaining ones do not run. Cost is O(k) for k targets.

Delegates are compared by target object and method, not by reference, so -= removes a subscription made with the same method on the same object.

It removes only the last matching entry: after d += M; d += M; d -= M; one M is still subscribed. Removing something that is not in the list does nothing, and removing the last entry makes the delegate null. Two separately written lambdas with identical text are different methods, so you cannot unsubscribe a lambda unless you kept it in a variable.

code.title: Func, Action, Predicate and a custom ref delegate

followUps:
No. Predicate<int> and Func<int, bool> have the same shape but are unrelated types, so there is no implicit conversion between them.

A lambda converts to either, but Func<int,bool> f = somePredicate; does not compile. Wrap it instead:

Func<int, bool> f = p.Invoke;       // method group
var f2 = new Func<int, bool>(p);   // explicit

The wrapper costs one extra delegate allocation and one extra call per invocation.

Since C# 10 a lambda with explicit parameter types has a natural type: the compiler picks Func or Action for it, so var f = (int x) => x * 2; is a Func<int,int>.

With a void body it becomes Action. If it has ref parameters or more than 16 parameters, the compiler invents a delegate type. Before C# 10, and when the parameter types are not written (var f = x => x;), a lambda has no type of its own and needs a target type such as Func<int,int> or Expression<...>.

code.title: Closure bug in a for loop and its fixes

followUps:
It generates a hidden class, called a display class (named like <>c__DisplayClass0_0), whose fields are the captured variables, and the lambda body becomes an instance method of it.

The enclosing method creates one instance when the captured variable's scope is entered and reads or writes the fields instead of locals. A loop variable declared in the for header lives in one instance for the whole loop; a variable declared inside the body gets a new instance each iteration. Lambdas that capture nothing are cached as static delegates. The cost is one heap allocation per scope entry.

A closure keeps its display class alive, and that class holds everything the lambda captured, so a small lambda can keep a large object reachable for as long as the lambda lives.

Two traps: a handler lambda added to a long-lived or static event that uses this captures the whole object, so it is never collected; and all lambdas in one scope share one display class, so a lambda that captures only a small value can still hold a big array captured by a sibling lambda. Remedies: unsubscribe, copy only what you need into a local, and mark lambdas static (C# 9) so the compiler forbids capture.

code.title: Event vs public delegate field

followUps:
Because it reads the event field once into a temporary, so the null check and the call use the same snapshot.

The older if (Clicked != null) Clicked(this, e); reads the field twice; if another thread unsubscribes the last handler in between, the second read is null and you get a NullReferenceException. Delegates are immutable, so the snapshot cannot change under you. One caveat: a handler removed just after the snapshot may still be called once.

Clicked?.Invoke(this, e);
// same as: var h = Clicked; if (h != null) h(this, e);

Write add and remove blocks yourself and store the handlers wherever you like.

private EventHandler _h;
public event EventHandler Changed {
    add    { lock (_lock) { _h += value; } }
    remove { lock (_lock) { _h -= value; } }
}

You raise it with _h?.Invoke(this, e). Typical reasons: your own locking, an EventHandlerList so a class with 50 events does not carry 50 fields, forwarding to an inner object, or validating subscribers. The compiler's automatic version already makes += and -= thread-safe, so custom accessors must keep that guarantee themselves.

code.title: Event handler leak through a static publisher

followUps:
No, not if the lambda truly captures nothing. The compiler then caches it as a static delegate with a null target, so the publisher holds no reference to your object.

The moment the lambda touches any instance member, even a single field, it captures this and the subscriber is kept alive by the publisher. For example Tick += () => Log("x"); is safe if Log is static but leaks if Log is an instance method. A lambda also cannot be unsubscribed later unless you stored it in a variable, which is another reason to use named methods for long-lived subscriptions.

In Rx, Subscribe returns an IDisposable, so the subscription is an object you can keep and dispose, instead of a pair of += and -= lines you must remember to match.

Disposing the token removes the observer from the source. You can store several in a CompositeDisposable and dispose them all in your own Dispose, or end a subscription automatically with TakeUntil. Rx itself comes from the System.Reactive package, but you can copy the idea without it: have Subscribe return a token whose Dispose unsubscribes (as in the event aggregator question).

code.title: Deferred execution: work happens at enumeration

followUps:
Streaming operators handle one element at a time with constant memory: Where, Select, Take, Skip, SelectMany, Concat, Zip. Buffering operators must read the whole source before returning the first item: OrderBy, GroupBy, Reverse, and the inner side of Join. Distinct streams but remembers every item seen.

Example: infinite.Where(IsPrime).Take(3) finishes, but infinite.OrderBy(x => x).Take(3) never returns. Operators like Count and Sum are not deferred; they consume everything immediately.

CA1851 is a .NET analyzer rule: "possible multiple enumerations of IEnumerable collection". It warns when the same IEnumerable<T> variable or parameter is enumerated more than once.

var n = items.Count();      // pass 1
foreach (var x in items) {} // pass 2

Each pass re-runs the whole deferred query, which may mean two database calls or two file reads, and it can give different results. Fix it by calling ToList() once, or by accepting IReadOnlyCollection<T> as the parameter type so callers must pass something already materialised.

code.title: yield return: lazy body and finally on break

followUps:
You cannot put yield return inside a try block that has a catch, nor inside a catch or finally block. A try/finally with yield return inside the try is allowed, and iterators cannot have ref or out parameters.

Workaround: put the risky call in a helper that has the try/catch and returns a flag or value, then yield outside it.

while (true) {
    int v; if (!TryNext(out v)) yield break;  // try/catch inside TryNext
    yield return v;
}

Because there is no "yield all", a recursive iterator re-yields each item through every enclosing iterator. With foreach (var x in Walk(child)) yield return x; an item found at depth d passes through d MoveNext calls.

For a balanced tree of n nodes that is about O(n log n) overall; for a degenerate chain of 1000 nodes it is roughly 500,000 calls, O(n squared). Fix: use one iterator with an explicit Stack<Node> (push root; pop, yield, push children), which is O(1) per element and O(depth) extra memory.

code.title: Query syntax and method syntax give the same result

followUps:
Query syntax is not tied to LINQ interfaces; the compiler just rewrites it into method calls and looks for methods with the right names (Select, Where, SelectMany...) as instance or extension methods.

So any type that has a suitable Select works with from. Example: if Box<T> has Box<R> Select<R>(Func<T,R> f), then from v in box select v + 1 compiles and calls it. This is how Rx, parallel LINQ and "maybe" types support the same syntax.

A left join in query syntax becomes GroupJoin followed by SelectMany with DefaultIfEmpty.

customers.GroupJoin(orders, c => c.Id, o => o.CustId,
        (c, g) => new { c, g })
    .SelectMany(x => x.g.DefaultIfEmpty(),
        (x, o) => new { x.c.Name, o });

The first from plus join ... into g is the GroupJoin, and the second from o in g.DefaultIfEmpty() is the SelectMany. For a customer without orders, o is null (for reference types), so check for it before use.

code.title: LINQ lambda call overhead vs a plain loop

followUps:
Count() on a List<T> is O(1); on a plain lazy IEnumerable<T> it is O(n).

LINQ first checks whether the source is an ICollection<T> and, if so, just returns its Count property. For a Where(...) result or an iterator method there is no stored count, so it walks every element and runs every lambda. For a list of 1,000,000 items that is instant versus a million MoveNext calls. If you only need to know whether anything exists, use Any(), which stops at the first element.

Replace the chain with a loop that writes into a pre-sized result, so only one allocation remains.

var r = new List<int>(a.Length);
for (int i = 0; i < a.Length; i++) {
    int x = a[i];
    if (x % 2 == 0) r.Add(x * 10);
}

Where and Select on an array allocate iterator objects and call a delegate per element; a capturing lambda adds a closure object too. Mark remaining lambdas static to forbid capture, work with Span<T> to avoid copies, and confirm the gain with BenchmarkDotNet's memory diagnoser.

code.title: Inner join vs left outer join with GroupJoin

followUps:
The inner (second) sequence is hashed into a lookup by key, and the outer sequence is streamed past it. That makes the join O(n + m) instead of the O(n * m) of nested loops.

It matters for memory and for when work happens: the inner side is read completely the first time you enumerate, and it must fit in memory, while the outer side is processed lazily. So put the smaller sequence (say 100 customers) as the inner one and the big one (1,000,000 orders) as the outer. Results come out in outer order, and for each outer item in inner order.

In LINQ to Objects, elements whose key is null never match anything, not even another null; this mirrors SQL, where NULL = NULL is not true.

Example: joining {"x", null} to {"x", null} with Join yields one pair, x|x. With GroupJoin the outer element with a null key is still returned, but with an empty group. If you do want nulls to match, project them to a sentinel key first, for example x => x ?? "".

code.title: Delegate vs expression tree

followUps:
The compiler decides from the target type. If the lambda is assigned to Expression<Func<...>>, it does not emit IL for the body; it emits code that builds a tree of objects describing it.

For Expression<Func<int,bool>> e = x => x > 5; it creates a ParameterExpression x, a ConstantExpression 5 and a GreaterThan node, wrapped in Expression.Lambda. You can read e.Body or call e.Compile() to get a normal delegate. Only expression-bodied lambdas convert; statement bodies, assignments and some newer syntax do not.

By default EF Core tracks every entity a query returns, keeping a snapshot so SaveChanges can detect edits. AsNoTracking() turns that off.

Read-only queries become faster and use less memory, because there is no change-tracker bookkeeping; with 10,000 rows the saving is noticeable. The trade-off: changing the returned objects will not be saved, and if the same row appears twice you get two separate objects instead of one shared instance (AsNoTrackingWithIdentityResolution() restores that). Use it for reports and list screens, not for edit-and-save flows.

code.title: Type-safe event aggregator with IDisposable tokens

followUps:
Make Publish look at the message's runtime type, its base classes and its interfaces, and call the handlers registered for each of them.

foreach (var t in TypesOf(msg.GetType()))   // cached per type
    if (map.TryGetValue(t, out var hs))
        foreach (var h in hs.ToArray()) h.DynamicInvoke(msg);

A handler for Action<OrderEvent> then also receives OrderShipped : OrderEvent. Cache the type list per concrete type in a ConcurrentDictionary so reflection runs once. Prefer a typed invoker over DynamicInvoke, which is slow.

Test it as plain behaviour with small, fast unit tests, using synchronous handlers so no timing is involved.

Cases: a subscriber receives a published message; after disposing its token it receives nothing; a handler that throws does not stop the others; a handler that subscribes, unsubscribes or publishes during Publish does not deadlock; messages of another type are not delivered. Add a stress test with Parallel.For doing 1,000 subscribes and publishes and assert exact counts. For weak-reference subscribers, drop the reference, call GC.Collect() and assert the handler no longer runs.

code.title: Multiple enumeration costs repeated round trips

followUps:
Count the SQL commands the endpoint sends and assert the number, so an accidental jump from 2 queries to 1,000 fails the build.

Run the endpoint in a test against a test database (for example in-memory SQLite) and register an EF Core DbCommandInterceptor that increments a counter in ReaderExecuting.

var counter = new CountingInterceptor();
await Call(report, counter);
Assert.Equal(2, counter.Commands);   // N+1 would be 1001

Use a fixed, realistic data size so a per-row query shows up clearly.

Drop LINQ when a profiler shows the code is hot, and keep it everywhere else. Typical cases: tight loops over millions of elements, code that must not allocate, and spans (which LINQ cannot use).

Another good case is several aggregates over the same data: Min(), Max() and Sum() read the data three times, one loop reads it once. LINQ is fine for 100 items or anything dominated by I/O, where its cost is invisible. Rule: measure first (BenchmarkDotNet or a profiler), because clearer code that is fast enough should win.

code.title: Output prediction: deferred Select over a changing list

followUps:
It prints 120, because the query reads the array's elements when it runs, not when it was built.

With arr = {1,2,3}, q = arr.Select(x => x * 10) and then arr[0] = 7, the sum is 70 + 20 + 30 = 120. Replacing an element is legal (arrays have no version check; only size changes are impossible). But if you reassign the variable, arr = new[] {9, 9}, the query still points at the old array and gives 60, because Select captured the original array object.

It throws InvalidOperationException ("Collection was modified; enumeration operation may not execute") on the next step after the first Add.

Example: foreach (var v in q) list.Add(v); processes the first element, adds it, and the next MoveNext sees that the list's internal version number changed and throws. List<T> keeps that counter to catch exactly this mistake. To add while looping, loop over a copy (list.ToList()) or collect additions in a second list and use AddRange after the loop.
